opus-5.5.text:
I think the two have to come together, and in a small team you feel that very directly. When there are only a handful of people working on something really important, like the inference systems or the infrastructure that a model depends on, there's nowhere to hide. If you're given the authority to make a decision, you also own the outcome, good or bad.

What I've learned is that authority, at least in the way I think about it, isn't really about being able to tell people what to do. It's more about having the right to make the call when there's uncertainty, when the team has discussed something and there's no obvious answer, and someone has to say, "Okay, we're going this way." That's the authority part. But the moment you make that call, the responsibility is yours. If it turns out to be the wrong direction, you can't say, "Well, the team decided." You have to be the one who stands up and says, "I made this choice, here's what we learned, here's how we fix it."

I think that actually makes people trust the leader more. In a fast-moving environment, people are willing to move quickly and take risks if they know that someone is going to take responsibility when things go wrong. If they feel like they'll be blamed for every mistake, they become conservative, and then you lose the speed that a small team is supposed to have.

The other side is that I try to give authority to the people on the team as well, and with it, responsibility. When someone owns a component end to end, they should be able to make decisions about it without asking me every time. That ownership is what makes people grow. But it only works if the authority is real. You can't give someone responsibility for something and then second-guess every decision they make, because then it's just accountability without power, and that's very frustrating for people.

So for me, the principle is pretty simple: authority and responsibility should always match. If they're out of balance in either direction, the team suffers. And as the leader, my job is to make sure that balance holds for everyone, including myself.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a question I think about a lot, actually, because at xAI the thing you notice very quickly is that you have far more responsibility than you have formal authority. The team is small, the goals are enormous, and nobody is going to hand you a title that makes people do what you say. So the first thing I learned is that authority isn't something you receive. It's something you earn, and you earn it by taking responsibility first.

When I started leading my team, I had this instinct from academia that leading meant deciding. You set the direction, you assign the work, people execute. That fell apart within weeks. The people I work with are extremely strong, often stronger than me in their specific area. If I tried to lead by assertion, they would just quietly route around me. What actually worked was being the person who would own the outcome unconditionally. If the training run failed at three in the morning, I was the one looking at the logs. If we missed a milestone, I didn't say "the team didn't deliver," I said "I didn't set this up right." And once people see that you'll absorb the downside, they start giving you the upside, which is trust, and trust is what authority actually is in a small team.

The second thing is that the two have to be matched, and the failure modes are symmetric. Authority without responsibility is the manager who makes calls and disappears when they go wrong. Everyone has worked for that person, and it corrodes a team fast. But responsibility without authority is just as bad. That's when you're accountable for a result but you can't change the priorities, can't move the compute, can't say no to a request from another group. That person burns out. So a lot of my job is making sure those stay aligned, both for me and for the people on my team. If I'm going to hold someone responsible for the data pipeline, they need real authority over it. They need to be able to push back on me.

And honestly, the thing that makes this workable at xAI is that the environment is very unforgiving about reality. The model either trains or it doesn't. The eval goes up or it doesn't. You can't hide behind process. That keeps everyone honest about where responsibility actually sits, because the outcome is visible to everybody within hours. I've come to think that's healthier than it sounds. It means authority stays tied to whoever is actually carrying the weight, rather than whoever argued best in a meeting.

astra-6.text:
For me, authority and responsibility have to go together. When you lead a small team, you need enough authority to make decisions, but you also have to own the consequences. You can’t make the call and then, when something goes wrong, say, “Well, that was someone else’s implementation.”

The same applies when you delegate. If I ask someone to own a problem, I need to give them room to decide how to solve it. If every decision still has to come through me, then I haven’t really given them ownership—I’ve just assigned them work.

In a small team, that matters a lot because the leader can easily become the bottleneck. My role is to make the goal and constraints clear, help when people get stuck, and take responsibility for the overall outcome. Authority is useful insofar as it helps you fulfill that responsibility.

sol-6.1.text:
I think authority and responsibility have to go together. If I’m asking someone to own a problem, I also need to give them the room to make decisions about it. Otherwise, they’re responsible for the result, but they don’t really control how to get there.

On a small team, that becomes especially important because the team lead can easily become the bottleneck. My role is to make the goal and the constraints clear, help resolve disagreements, and make sure people have what they need. It shouldn’t be that every decision has to come through me.

And delegation doesn’t mean I stop being accountable. If something goes wrong, I need to ask whether I gave enough context, whether the priorities were clear, and whether I put the right support in place. To me, authority is useful because it lets you take responsibility and help other people succeed.
